text:
Forensic findings CASEID FILE NOTE
1) Domain context:
Institutional records offices typically maintain student files through centralized document management systems, employing sequential accession numbering and standardized metadata fields. Originals are retained in physical or digitized repositories with access controls tied to role-based permissions. Audit trails log creation, modification, and retrieval events with timestamps and user identifiers. Verification workflows cross-reference applicant submissions against source-system records, checking identifier formats, date plausibility, and institutional correspondence patterns. Registrar verification channels include direct confirmation calls, secure electronic exchanges, and physical inspection of seals, signatures, and paper stock. Retention schedules classify records by sensitivity, with academic credentials subject to permanent or long-term retention and periodic integrity reviews.

2) What occurred:
The actor authored a document styled as an academic transcript, populating fields for course titles, grades, credit hours, dates of attendance, and cumulative grade point average with values consistent with the target degree program. The actor produced a companion document styled as a diploma, incorporating institutional name, degree title, conferral date, and placeholder fields for signatures and seals. Both documents were formatted to match the target institution's standard templates. The actor identified the employer's verification channel and prepared response scripts for anticipated registrar inquiries.

3) Materials/access observed:
The actor utilized publicly available institutional branding materials, degree program descriptions, and sample credential layouts obtained from open web sources. Template structures were extracted from publicly posted sample transcripts and diploma facsimiles. The actor referenced standard academic grading scales and typical course numbering conventions for the relevant field of study. No privileged system access was obtained; all materials were sourced from public-facing institutional communications and third-party repositories.

4) Indicators & artifacts:
Artifacts included two document files (transcript and diploma) with metadata indicating creation dates, software application signatures, and absence of original institutional document management system identifiers. The transcript exhibited sequential course numbering and grade distributions matching typical program completion patterns but lacking individual course-level audit trail references. The diploma displayed signature and seal elements as digital images rather than original handwritten or embossed artifacts. Both documents contained institution names and degree titles matching the target employer's requirements. Verification channel references indicated anticipated response paths through standard registrar confirmation workflows. Document creation metadata did not originate from institutional document management systems. Date fields showed internal consistency but no corresponding entries in institutional student information systems accessible through public verification channels.
